content: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is frequently identified through the presence of elevated urinary albumin excretion, known as albuminuria, or a reduced estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), both of which are markers of kidney damage. Diabetic kidney disease, a specific type of CKD that arises as a complication of diabetes, impacts approximately 20-40% of adults living with diabetes. This condition generally manifests within 10 to 20 years following the onset of diabetes. However, in individuals with type 2 diabetes, CKD may already be present at the time of diabetes diagnosis. The progression of CKD in patients with diabetes significantly heightens the risk of cardiovascular complications and contributes to increased health care expenditures. In its most severe form, CKD can progress to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), a condition that necessitates either dialysis or kidney transplantation for survival.
